tagline.text: The island where jade lakes and sunken warships sleep beneath the sea

children.text: Coron, on Busuanga Island in northern Palawan, is famous for Kayangan Lake and Barracuda Lake tucked inside limestone islands, and Twin Lagoon. Japanese warships sunk during World War II form a world-class wreck-diving destination, and there's also Mount Tapyas viewpoint and a seawater hot spring to enjoy.

Coron is a city in the Calamian Islands north of the main Palawan island. What travelers call "Coron" usually refers to Coron town at the southeastern end of Busuanga Island, Coron Island just offshore, and the surrounding islands all together. Coron Island, the center of the trip, is covered in sharp limestone peaks, with around ten hidden lakes inside the island and lagoons ringed by cliffs along the coast.

Coron Island is the ancestral territory of the indigenous Tagbanwa people, formally recognized by the Philippine government as their ancestral domain. So major sites like Kayangan Lake, Barracuda Lake, and Twin Lagoon are managed directly by the Tagbanwa community, which charges entrance fees and sets swimming zones and visiting hours. Most of the island's lakes are considered sacred sites and are off-limits to visitors.
Coron has another face beneath the waves. On
September 24, 1944

, a Japanese fleet hiding in Coron Bay was attacked by US Navy carrier aircraft, sinking over ten ships at once, including supply ships and a seaplane tender. The wrecks of the seaplane tender Akitsushima, the supply ship Irako, and the tanker Okikawa Maru remain relatively intact at depths of
, making Coron one of the world's top ten wreck-diving destinations. Even without diving, you can see the Skeleton Wreck in shallow water by snorkeling.

Where El Nido centers on beaches and lagoons, Coron offers a wider range of experiences — lakes, wrecks, viewpoints, and hot springs. It especially suits divers, snorkeling enthusiasts, and travelers after dramatic scenic photos.
The highlight of a Coron Island tour: climb steps for about
10–15 minutes
to a viewpoint overlooking the bay between limestone peaks, then descend the other side to swim in the clear lake. Lines form at the viewpoint for photos, so it's best to go early.
A curious lake where fresh and salt water form layers, with water temperature shifting sharply with depth. It's also known as a freediving and diving spot.
Swim through a narrow gap in the rocks, or cross a ladder, and a second lagoon appears. You can swim across at low tide, and use the ladder at high tide.
Diving to explore the remains of World War II Japanese vessels such as the Akitsushima, Irako, and Okikawa Maru. Diving inside the hulls is only for experienced divers with wreck-diving training.

blocks.title: Snorkeling the Skeleton Wreck and coral gardens

children.text: With shallow water letting you see the wreck's skeleton even from the surface, the Skeleton Wreck and coral gardens are recommended for non-divers.
Climb more than 700 steps up the hill behind Coron town and watch the sun set over the sea and islands beside the large cross. The climb takes about
20–30 minutes
A seawater hot spring bubbling up beside a mangrove near the coast, where you can soak away the day's fatigue in water at about 38–40°C. It's cooler and more pleasant after dark.

to

From
June
to
October
is the rainy and typhoon season. As with Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda), which struck Coron in

Coron town's center is the most convenient place to stay, with a cluster of guesthouses and mid-range hotels (about
per night), close to tour pickups and restaurants. For sea views, resorts on the outskirts hills or the coast (about
per night) are good. For a quiet island getaway, an island resort around Busuanga is an option, though it requires boat transport and costs more.

Coron town has many seafood restaurants. It's popular to pick fresh fish, shrimp, squid, and crab and have them grilled or cooked in chili sauce; Coron specialties include cashews (Palawan is a cashew-growing region) and seafood dishes. Cheap restaurants near the public market serve Filipino home cooking for about
per person. Island tour lunches usually feature grilled fish, pork barbecue, rice, and fruit.
Town has a few ATMs, but cash often runs out on weekends and in peak season. It's best to bring enough cash before you arrive.
Site entrance fees are often not included in tour prices, so confirm this when booking.
Popular tours crowd Kayangan Lake at
. Reversing the tour order or requesting an early departure gives a much more relaxed visit.
The steps at Kayangan Lake are steep and slippery, so sturdy-soled shoes are better than aqua shoes or sandals.
Before wreck diving, tell the dive center exactly your certification level and depth limit.
Vans to the airport are often scheduled well over
2 hours
before your flight, so it's best to confirm the pickup time in advance.
Smart and Globe signals are good in town but drop out almost entirely during island tours.
Kayangan Lake can be entered only between
7 AM and 4 PM
, and the admission fee of about
includes a life jacket and a local guide. If you arrive at
just after opening, you will barely have to queue at the viewpoint.

Coron Island's lakes and lagoons are sacred Tagbanwa territory. Swimming outside designated zones, noise, and littering are banned, and rules and fees can change by community decision, so check the latest notices.
Wreck interiors are dangerous due to their maze-like structure and silt, so divers without the proper training should never enter.
A life vest is recommended at Barracuda Lake and Kayangan Lake, and required if you're not a confident swimmer.
The limestone rocks are sharp and easy to cut your feet on, so wearing aqua shoes is a good idea.
Tours and ferries can be cancelled suddenly during typhoon and monsoon season, so leave buffer time in your schedule.

of diving.
